motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code, Chapter 7 Parks, Trails, and Special Events; Chapter 16 Subdivisions and Chapter 17 Zoning. Grants Coordinator/Management Analyst Natalie Winterton and Finance/Management Analyst Terrence Dela Pena presented the item. Changes made based upon feedback from the September Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting- April 25, 2023 Page 5 of9 6, 2022 City Council meeting include a one-year to nine-month landscape requirement for developments, the requirements applying only to new builds, and small wording improvements. Residents have requested that the City take the necessary steps so they can qualify for Flip the Strip and other programs. The Central Utah Water Conservancy District (CUWCD) has said that certain requirements must be met to continue in a working relationship with them. This is the start of a multi-pronged effort to conserve water in the City. Benefits of the program: • Builders: Qualify for rebates from the State of Utah for installing more water-wise landscapes. • Residents: Qualify for Flip the Strip and other State relandscaping rebates. • City: Qualifies for continued business with the CUWCD and additional grants. Proposed amendments to Eagle Mountain Municipal Code: • Chapters 16 and 17 -minor changes; • 17 .10.030 -adds a definition for ambiguous concepts; • 17.25.050 -makes standards more consistent and increases the time for builders to install landscaping; • 17.60.030 -clarifies that new requirements are only applicable to new builds and defines significant relandscaping; • 17.60.040 - clarifies that new requirements are only applicable to new builds, requires Water Sense smart irrigation, prohibits nonfunctional turf, and adds irrigation requirements; • 17.60.070 -deletes standards made unnecessary by the amendments; • 17 .60.080 - deletes standards made unnecessary by the amendments and corrects grammatical errors; • 17 .60.090-adds new requirements to align the standards with CUWCD recommendations and emphasizes that the standards will only apply to new builds; • 17 .60.110 -clarifies language; and • 17 .60.110 -deletes the table that is inapplicable with the new standards . Discussion ensued regarding the challenges of measuring and enforcing changes to significant re landscaping as defined as more than 75% of the lot's total landscaping and considerations for phased projects. Because the item was not listed as a public hearing on the agenda, the Commission confirmed with staff that the item had been noticed as a public hearing. Commissioner Everett opened the public hearing at 7:42 p.m. As there were no comments, he closed the hearing. Discussion supported the benefit of the changes despite enforceability difficulties. Commissioner Everett noted the importance of the City's partnership with the CUWCD and agrees with the benefits to the residents and City noted in the staff report. Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting - April 25, 2023 Page 6 of9 Commissioner Allen cited l 7.60.090(O), "At maturity, landscape areas shall have enough plant material to create at least 50% living plant cover at the ground plane, not including tree canopies." He feels that requiring 50% living plant cover might be too high and 25% would be more appropriate. Commissioner Pengra agreed. Commissioner Pengra expressed concern with requiring a Water Sense smart irrigation controller and the specification for drip irrigation systems due to enforceability. He feels that mulch is as effective as a weed barrier and is more environmentally friendly. Ms. Winterton explained that the requirement for 50% living plant cover, Water Sense smart irrigation controllers, and the specification for drip irrigation systems came from CUWCD materials; however, she is unsure if they would be amenable to a higher or lower percentage of living plant cover. Artificial turf is not contemplated in the current standards. Discussion ensued regarding the consistency in collecting and refunding the $2,000 cash escrow retained until landscaping is completed, landscaping finished outside of the allotted timeframe by individual residents rather than developers, and the City installing landscaping for properties out of compliance. Commissioner Pengra stated that he has objections to the collecting and holding of the escrow money due to possible issues with managing and returning the funds. He feels landscaping compliance problems would be better addressed through Code Enforcement and the judicial process. Mr. Mumford explained that there is a separate account for the escrows and the payment, tracking, and refunding processes. The Planning Department has struggled with balancing the requirements and procedures. He suggested that the City consider a landscaping installation incentivization rather than being punitive. Discussion ensued regarding the benefits and challenges of requiring individuals to deposit funds in an escrow when building their own homes compared to professional builders. City Attorney Marcus Draper explained that developers can be held accountable for landscaping installation through their development agreement and would be motivated by the potential for litigation over the escrow amount whereas individual residents would likely be motivated by having their money refunded. Commissioner Everett suggested including a provision to allow for extensions of the landscaping installation timeframe for extenuating circumstances. Commissioner Bergener noted a correction to the enumeration to 17.60.040(1) to remove the superfluous 3.
motions.motion: Commissioner Pengra moved to recommend approval to the City Council of an ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah amending the Eagle Mountain Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting - April 25, 2023 Page 7 of9 Municipal Code, Chapter 7 Parks, Trails, and Special Events; Chapter 16 Subdivisions and Chapter 17 Zoning with the following changes: 1. The number 3 shall be removed from the section 17.60.040(1) title; and 2. Staff shall work to include a provision to 17.25.0S0(A) to allow the City to provide extensions to individual lot owners if they can show meaningful progress on their landscaping. Commissioner Allen seconded the motion.
